claim: Colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen and Set staining was found in testis cells.

evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Strong Set staining was found in Fshr-ZsGreen-positive spermatogonia.
source: We found strong Set staining in Fshr-ZsGreen-positive spermatogonia, as indicated by empty white arrowheads (Figure 2C-b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the arterioles of the testis.

claim: Single RNA molecule-fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed Fshr expression in the Leydig cells using antisense probe.
source: Because of RNA in situ hybridization as the gold standard method for visualizing RNA expression and localization in cells, tissue sections, and whole organs (Young et al., 2020; Levsky and Singer, 2003), we further carried out single RNA molecule-fluorescence in situ hybridization to confirm Fshr expression in the Leydig cells, using antisense probe for identifying Fshr expression in the sections of Fshr-ZsGreen and B6 mice, whereas its sense probe was used as a negative control (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-smFISH data shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: The majority of TM3 cells stained for lower Fshr, only a few cells stained relatively higher Fshr.
source: Additionally, we also examined Fshr expression by IF in Leydig cell line TM3 (Mather, 1980) and found that the majority of TM3 cells stained for lower Fshr, only a few cells stained relatively higher Fshr (Figure 2E-a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fshr expression was observed located in the nuclei of TM3 cells.

The results showed that Fshr expression was similar in the testes and ovaries of both types of mice, indicating that the insertion of P2A-ZsGreen did not disrupt Fshr expression in Fshr-ZsGreen mice.
evidence: This is supported by the ddRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The insertion of P2A-ZsGreen did not disrupt Fshr expression in Fshr-ZsGreen mice.
source: The results showed that Fshr expression was similar in the testes and ovaries of both types of mice, indicating that the insertion of P2A-ZsGreen did not disrupt Fshr expression in Fshr-ZsGreen mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ddRT-PCR comparison data.

claim: Lower expression of Fshr was observed in chondrocytes in the epiphyseal growth plate compared to its expression in cells located in the sponge area above or under the growth plate.
source: In the epiphyseal growth plate, we observed lower expression of Fshr in chondrocytes, as indicated by two dotted lines, compared to its expression in cells located in the sponge area above or under the dotted lines (Figure 3A-a).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fshr was expressed in the columns of chondrocytes from the resting zone to the transformation zone.
source: At higher magnification, Fshr was expressed in the columns of chondrocytes from the resting zone to the transformation zone (Figure 3A-e).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fshr was brightly expressed in osteoblasts and osteoclasts in the metaphyseal trabeculae.
source: In contrast, we found that Fshr was brightly expressed in osteoblasts and osteoclasts in the metaphyseal trabeculae, which were recognized based on nuclear DAPI staining - osteoblasts were stained with a single DAPI nucleus, while osteoclasts contained more than two DAPI-stained nuclei (Figure 3A-c and d).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells on the surfaces of trabeculae in bone marrow and cortical bone clearly expressed Fshr-ZsGreen.
source: Similarly, we further observed that these cells on the surfaces of trabeculae in bone marrow and cortical bone also clearly expressed Fshr-ZsGreen, as shown in Figure 3A-e and f (trabeculae) and Figure 3A-g and h (cortex).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was noted in osteocytes embedded in trabecular and cortical bone, as well as in the periosteum.
source: Importantly, we noted Fshr-ZsGreen expression in osteocytes (indicated by empty white arrowheads, Figure 3A-d, g, and h), the most abundant cell in the skeleton. These were embedded in trabecular and cortical bone, as well as in the periosteum (P) (Figure 3A-h).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Colocalization of Fshr expression with osteocalcin staining was observed in chondrocytes in the transforming zone, in cuboid and nucleated osteoblasts and bone lining cells on the trabecular and endosteal surfaces, cortical bone, and osteocytes within the mineralized matrix.
source: To confirm the identification of osteoblasts/osteocytes and osteoclasts that expressed Fshr, we performed IF staining using an antibody against osteocalcin, a marker of osteoblasts (Karsenty, 2017). As shown in Figure 1B, we observed colocalization of Fshr expression with osteocalcin staining in chondrocytes in the transforming zone, as indicated by white arrows (Figure 3B-a), in cuboid and nucleated osteoblasts and bone lining cells on the trabecular and endosteal surfaces (Figure 3B-b and c), cortical bone, and osteocytes within the mineralized matrix (Figure 3B-b, c, and e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Multinucleated Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells were stained positively for Trap located on the surface of the resorptive bays or areas adjacent to the trabecular bone.
source: To identify osteoclasts, we performed fluorescence immunostaining with an antibody against Trap, an osteoclast marker (Lindunger et al., 1990). Osteoclasts were recognized by positive staining for TRAP with more than two DAPI-stained nuclei. Multinucleated Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells were stained positively for Trap located on the surface of the resorptive bays or areas adjacent to the trabecular bone (Figure 3B-e and f).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells were identified as stem/progenitor cells located in the bone marrow, growth plate/articular cartilage, and periosteum using stem markers CD34 or CD133.

Using these well-known stem markers, we identified Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells as stem/progenitor cells located in the bone marrow, growth plate/articular cartilage, and periosteum, as shown in Figure 2C-a, b, c, e, and d, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

We noticed a significant drop of Fshr expression in osteocytes in Fshr cKO mice when tamoxifen was intraperitoneally administrated to the mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: An increased thickness of cortex was triggered by Fshr cKO in osteocytes.

evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

source: As expected, we found Fshr-ZsGreen expression in adipocytes of the frozen sectioned inguinal WAT, as shown in the left panel of Figure 4A at a low magnification (×40), which was further confirmed under a higher magnification (×400) in the three representative areas, demonstrating that Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in the cellular membranes of individual adipocytes (Figure 4A-a, b, and c).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells in WAT were stained positively for Ucp1.
source: To confirm adipocyte identification, we performed IF with an antibody against mouse Ucp1 (Liu et al., 2017) to recognize adipocytes, showing that the majority of Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells were stained positively for Ucp1, and found two types of Fshr+ adipocyte populations: one with colocalization of the two markers only in the membrane (indicated by empty white arrowheads) and another with two markers in both the membrane and cytoplasm (indicated by white arrows) (Figure 4B-a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in arterioles in adipose tissue.

evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed not only in the cellular membranes but also in areas of cytoplasm close to the membranes in BAT.
source: We further examined Fshr-ZsGreen expression in BAT. Fshr-ZsGreen was observed across the whole section of examined BAT at a lower magnification (Figure 3A-a). At a higher magnification (×400), three representative areas are presented, as shown in Figure 3A-b, c, and d, in which Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed not only in the cellular membranes but also in areas of cytoplasm close to the membranes, as indicated by white arrows (Figure 4C-b, c, and d).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was colocalized with Ucp1 in brown adipose tissue cells.
source: Furthermore, we also performed IF with three antibodies against Ucp1, Th, and Peri to identify brown cells and peripheral fibers in the Fshr-positive section. We found that several areas in the section were strongly stained for Ucp1 at low magnification (×40), as shown in Figure 4D-a. Under higher magnifications of ×400 and ×1000, we colocalized Fshr-ZsGreen with Ucp1 in the three representative areas, in which some locations had higher Fshr-ZsGreen expression and others had higher Ucp1 expression (Figure 4D-a, b, and d).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neural fibers stained positively and surrounded Fshr-ZsGreen-positive arterioles in BAT.
source: To examine whether peripheral neural fibers express Fshr, we used antibodies against Th and Peri that can recognize peripheral neural fibers. We found that neural fibers stained positively and surrounded Fshr-ZsGreen-positive arterioles in BAT (Figure 4E-a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in the nodes of Ranvier of TH-stained small neural fibers.
source: In addition, Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in the nodes of Ranvier of TH-stained small neural fibers (indicated by empty red arrows, Figure 4E-e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen and Peri staining was noted in large neural fibers.
source: We further confirmed Fshr-ZsGreen expression in peripheral neural fibers by IF with an antibody against peripherin (Peri), which is a type III intermediate filament protein found predominantly in peripheral nerves, specifically in sensory and autonomic neurons (Figure 4F). We noted colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen and Peri staining in large neural fibers (Figure 4F-b, d, and e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both markers for peripheral neural fibers were expressed in the cytoplasm of BAT cells, in which Fshr-ZsGreen was strongly expressed.
source: Interestingly, we observed that both markers for peripheral neural fibers were also expressed in the cytoplasm of BAT cells, in which Fshr-ZsGreen was strongly expressed (Figure 4E-b, c, and f; Figure 4F-e, c, and f).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining with Fshr antibody in white and BAT adipose sections of B6 mice showed a similar expression pattern as seen in Fshr-ZsGreen mice.
source: To further ensure Fshr expression in adipose tissues, we also performed IF staining with Fshr antibody in white and BAT adipose sections of B6 mice. The results showed the similar expression pattern as seen in Fshr-ZsGreen mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in the myocardium.
source: To examine Fshr expression in the cardiovascular system, we used the heart and aorta as key organs/tissues to detect Fshr-ZsGreen expression. As expected, we observed strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the myocardium (Figure 5A-a) and large muscular arteries (a representative is shown in Figure 5A-b).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in large muscular arteries.
source: As expected, we observed strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the myocardium (Figure 5A-a) and large muscular arteries (a representative is shown in Figure 5A-b).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was highly expressed in cardiomyocytes in longitudinal and transverse orientations of the myocardium, which were positively stained for α-SMA.
source: With IF staining for α-SMA, we imaged several areas of both heart and blood vessels, as shown in the left image of the upper panel (×40). In the heart, we observed that Fshr-ZsGreen was highly expressed in cardiomyocytes in longitudinal and transverse orientations of the myocardium, which were positively stained for α-SMA (Figure 6B-a, b, and c).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in the endothelial layer of arterioles between muscle fibers.
source: At a magnification of ×1000, it was also expressed in the endothelial layer of arterioles between muscle fibers (Figure 5B-i).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was found in adipose tissue around the blood vessels, and the adipocytes morphologically appeared to be brown adipose cells.
source: In addition to the cardiomyocytes, we also observed Fshr-ZsGreen in α-SMA-stained smooth muscles and endothelial cells of large blood vessels above the heart (Figure 7B-d). Interestingly, we found Fshr-ZsGreen in adipose tissue around the blood vessels, and the adipocytes morphologically appeared to be brown adipose cells, as the majority of these brown-like cells were full of ZsGreen-positive cytoplasm, instead of single large fat droplets with Fshr-ZsGreen expression in cellular membranes (Figure 5B-c, d, e, and j).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Bright Fshr-ZsGreen expression with slightly weak staining for α-SMA was observed in the layer of endothelial cells of the large vein.
source: Furthermore, we observed bright Fshr-ZsGreen expression with slightly weak staining for α-SMA in the layer of endothelial cells of the large vein in Figure 5B-f and h.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A thin layer of endothelial cells (tunica intima) and stronger Fshr-ZsGreen expression with positive staining for α-SMA was observed in the large artery (tunica media).
source: In contrast to the vein, we observed a thin layer of endothelial cells (tunica intima) and stronger Fshr-ZsGreen expression with positive staining for α-SMA in the large artery (tunica media); Fshr-ZsGreen was also present in the cells in the tunica adventitia (Figure 5B-k).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in neural fiber clusters that were in adipose tissue in frozen sections of hearts.
source: In frozen sections of hearts, we observed strong Fshr-ZsGreen expression in neural fiber clusters that were in adipose tissue, as shown in Figure 5B-g and m.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was found in the layer of endothelium (tunica intima), which showed visible positive staining for EMCN.
source: Using an antibody against EMCN, a marker for endothelial cells, we further confirmed Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the layer of endothelium (tunica intima), which showed visible positive staining for EMCN when imaged at ×400 and ×1000 (Figure 5C-a, b, and d).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen+ cardiomyocytes and smooth muscles under the endothelial layer were positive for EMCN staining.
source: In addition, Fshr-ZsGreen+ cardiomyocytes and smooth muscles under the endothelial layer were positive for EMCN staining (Figure 5C-a, b, and c).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen+ smooth muscle fibers were strongly stained for α-SMA in the first layer of SM close to the endothelium in the ascending aorta, where the second layer of smooth muscle was relatively weak for staining with α-SMA.
source: In addition to large blood vessels on the heart, we also took a close look at the ascending aorta. We obtained two types of sections with longitudinal and transverse orientations for IFs with the two antibodies as above. In both sections, we found that Fshr-ZsGreen+ smooth muscle fibers were strongly stained for α-SMA in the first layer of SM close to the endothelium, where the second layer of smooth muscle was relatively weak for staining with α-SMA (Figures 5D-a and 6B-e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 5D.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was present at the endothelium, which was costained positively for α-SMA in the ascending aorta.
source: Fshr-ZsGreen was also present at the endothelium, which was costained positively for α-SMA (Figure 6A-a and B-e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Positive staining for EMCN was in the upper part of Fshr-ZsGreen+ endothelial cells facing the lumen of the examined blood vessels.
source: Using an anti-EMCN antibody, we noticed that positive staining was in the upper part of Fshr-ZsGreen+ endothelial cells facing the lumen of the examined blood vessels (Figure 5A-c and B-f).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the areas of subendothelial connective tissue and tunica media (smooth muscle), but these areas were not stained for EMCN.
source: In addition to Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the endothelium of the tunica intima, it was also observed in the areas of subendothelial connective tissue and tunica media (smooth muscle), but these areas were not stained for EMCN (Figure 5A-c and B-f).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: High Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in the lung.
source: To identify whether Fshr is expressed in epithelial cells, we first detected Fshr-ZsGreen in the lung. Unexpectedly, we observed high Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the lung (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was brightly expressed in the columnar epithelium of the respiratory conducting zone/tract, including the trachea, bronchus, bronchi, and bronchiole.
source: Fshr-ZsGreen was brightly expressed in the columnar epithelium of the respiratory conducting zone/tract, including the trachea, bronchus, bronchi, and bronchiole, at low magnification (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed not only in the columnar epithelium but also in the bronchial gland and alveoli.
source: At higher magnifications, it was clearly shown that Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed not only in the columnar epithelium but also in the bronchial gland and alveoli (Figure 6A-a, b, d, e, f, and g).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the alveoli, Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the respiratory portion of both type I and II cells.
source: In the alveoli, Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the respiratory portion of both type I and II cells, as indicated by empty arrowheads and white arrows, respectively (Figure 6A-d and h).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Colocalization of Fshr-GFP with PD-L1 staining confirmed the identification of respiratory cells.
source: We confirmed the identification of respiratory cells by IF with an anti-PD-L1 antibody, which showed the colocalization of Fshr-GFP with PD-L1 (Guo et al., 2024) staining (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: High expression of Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the proximal and distal convoluted tubules in the kidney.
source: Then, we aimed to examine Fshr expression in epithelial cells of the kidney. In the frozen section of the kidney, it was astonishing to observe high expression of Fshr-ZsGreen in the proximal and distal convoluted tubules (Figure 6B-e and f), whereas relatively weak expression was observed in the glomerular capillaries at different magnifications (Figure 6B-e and f at ×400 and Figure 6B-g at ×1000).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Relatively weak expression of Fshr-ZsGreen was observed in the glomerular capillaries.
source: In the frozen section of the kidney, it was astonishing to observe high expression of Fshr-ZsGreen in the proximal and distal convoluted tubules (Figure 6B-e and f), whereas relatively weak expression was observed in the glomerular capillaries at different magnifications (Figure 6B-e and f at ×400 and Figure 6B-g at ×1000).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in the endothelial layer of the arteriole in the kidney tissue.
source: Again, we observed Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the endothelial layer of the arteriole in the kidney tissue (Figure 6B-h).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen with positive staining for Col1a1 was observed in the kidney.
source: We also observed colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen with positive staining for Col1a1 (Kuroda et al., 2014) in the kidney (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was observed in the hepatocytes and arteries inside the hepatocytes, which were positively stained for Col1a1 or CD31.
source: With the power of Fshr-ZsGreen, we characterized Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the liver. We observed Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the hepatocytes and arteries inside the hepatocytes, which were positively stained for Col1a1 or CD31 (Wang et al., 2021; Ismail et al., 2003), respectively (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7A and B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen is weakly expressed inside large nerve fibers but strongly expressed in small neural fibers and shows a costaining pattern with KCBMA1.
source: Although it is weakly expressed inside large nerve fibers, Fshr-ZsGreen is strongly expressed in small neural fibers and shows a costaining pattern with KCBMA1 (Simms and Zamponi, 2014), a marker used for the detection of peripheral nerve fibers (Figure 7C, indicated by white arrowhead, whereas large nerve fibers are indicated by white arrows).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed not only in acinar cells but also in islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
source: We then examined Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the pancreas and found that it was expressed not only in acinar cells but also in islets of Langerhans at low and high magnifications (Figure 8A-a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in both α- and β-cells as well as acinar cells in the pancreas.
source: We then confirmed the identification of α- and β-cells by IFs with antibodies against NG3, insulin, or glucagon. The imaging results clearly demonstrated that Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in both α- and β-cells as well as acinar cells at ×400 and ×1000 magnifications, respectively (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was found in both follicular cells and parafollicular cells (C-cells) in the thyroid.
source: Regarding Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the thyroid, we found Fshr-ZsGreen in both follicular cells and parafollicular cells (C-cells) at low and high magnifications (×400 and ×1000) (Figure 9A-a, b, c, d, and e).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Follicular cells were stained positively for Tshr in the nuclei in the thyroid.
source: We further used an anti-Tshr receptor antibody to confirm Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells, which showed that follicular cells were stained positively for Tshr in the nuclei, as indicated by dotted circles and white arrowheads, and C-cells were indicated by white arrows (Figure 9-b to e).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in hair follicle (HF) and sweat gland cells and fibroblasts in the dermis and hypodermis in thick skin from the tail.
source: Next, to examine Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the skin, we used two types of skin sections: thick skin from the tail and thin skin from the abdomen (Figure 10A-a and b). Although a dermis layer was not included in the image taken for a thick sample, we observed that Fshr-ZsGreen was expressed in hair follicle (HF) and sweat gland cells and fibroblasts in the dermis and hypodermis (Figure 10A-a).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was present in HFs and fibroblasts in the dermis and keratinocytes in the epidermis of the thin skin.
source: Similarly, Fshr-ZsGreen was present in HFs and fibroblasts in the dermis and keratinocytes in the epidermis of the thin skin (Figure 10A-b).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: CD34 staining was colocalized with cells with Fshr-ZsGreen in Bulge as quiescent stem cells and in the dermal papilla (DP) and epidermis as active stem/progenitor cells.
source: As we detected Fshr-ZsGreen expression in HFs, we wondered whether stem cells in HFs express Fshr-ZsGreen. To address this question, we carried out IF with an antibody against CD34, a stem cell marker. Not surprisingly, we found that CD34 staining was colocalized with cells with Fshr-ZsGreen in Bulge as quiescent stem cells and in the dermal papilla (DP) and epidermis as active stem/progenitor cells, as shown in Figure 10B-a and b.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was present in the muscle fibers, in which one type had higher Fshr-ZsGreen expression and another type had lower Fshr-ZsGreen expression in skeletal muscle.
source: We then detected Fshr expression in skeletal muscle (gastrocnemius), followed by IF staining using three antibodies against α-SMA, PAX7, and TH for the identification of satellite cells and peripheral nerve fibrils. We observed Fshr-ZsGreen across the muscle sections at a lower magnification of ×40 (Figure 11a). At higher magnifications, we found that Fshr-ZsGreen was present in the muscle fibers, in which one type had higher Fshr-ZsGreen expression (indicated by white arrowheads) and another type had lower Fshr-ZsGreen expression (Figure 11-b to h).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen was highly expressed in satellite cells stained positively for either αSMA or PAX7 in both longitudinal and transverse sections of skeletal muscle.
source: Fshr-ZsGreen was also highly expressed in satellite cells stained positively for either αSMA (Figure 11-b to e) or PAX7 (Figure 11-f and g) in both longitudinal and transverse sections, as indicated by white arrows.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was detected in the peripheral neural fibers identified by positive staining for TH, which were around vascular structures in the muscle tissue.
source: In addition, we detected Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the peripheral neural fibers identified by positive staining for TH, which were around vascular structures in the muscle tissue, as indicated by red arrowheads (Figure 11-h and i).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Fshr was highly expressed in trabeculae and cells in both red and white pulps (RP and WP) of the spleen.
source: To detect Fshr expression in immune cells, we examined Fshr-ZsGreen expression in the spleen and bone marrow using antibodies against CD11b and CD3, as integrin αM (CD11b) is expressed in myeloid-lineage cells such as monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils and in lymphoid cells such as NK cells and B-1 cells (Springer, 1994), while CD3 marks T-cells (Chatenoud and Bluestone, 2007). We imaged frozen sections of the spleen under magnifications of ×40, ×400, and ×1000 and observed that Fshr-ZsGreen was highly expressed in trabeculae and cells in both red and white pulps (RP and WP).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 12A and B.

claim: Fshr is expressed in immune cells, such as monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, NK cells, B-cells, and T-cells.
source: The Fshr-ZsGreen-positive cells were further identified by IFs with antibodies against CD11B or CD3, indicating that Fshr is expressed in immune cells, such as monocytes/macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, NK cells, B-cells, and T-cells (Figure 12A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 12A and B.

claim: Fshr-ZsGreen expression was confirmed in macrophages of bone marrow, which were identified with anti-CD4/80 antibody.
source: In addition, we further confirmed Fshr-ZsGreen expression in macrophages of bone marrow, which were identified with anti-CD4/80 antibody, as shown in two representative images of BM-one from an area located in the center of bone marrow (Figure 12C-a) and another close to cortical bone (Figure 12C-b) at ×1000 magnification (empty white arrows indicate the colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen and CD11B, CD3, or CD4/80 in the RPs, while white arrows point to their colocalization in the WPs).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Fshr expression was observed across the brain sections in astrocytes, microglia, and neurons, as well as neuronal fibers (synapses or projections).
source: Finally, we examined Fshr-ZsGreen expression and its colocalization with markers for either astrocytes, microglia, or neurons in the brain. As expected, we observed Fshr expression across the brain sections and the three representatives from the olfactory bulbs, pallidum, and hippocampus (CA3) are shown in Figure 12, demonstrating that Fshr is indeed expressed in astrocytes (Figure 13-a to c), microglia (Figure 12-d to f), and neurons (Figure 13-g to j), as well as neuronal fibers (synapses or projections).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen with positive staining for Fshr was observed in all the examined tissues, including bone, BAT, thyroid, cardiac muscle, kidney, liver, lung, aorta, ovary, and testis.
source: As shown in Figure 14A, in all the examined tissues, including bone, BAT, thyroid, cardiac muscle, kidney, liver, lung, aorta, ovary, and testis, we observed colocalization of Fshr-ZsGreen with positive staining for Fshr, further confirming the specific expression of Fshr-ZsGreen in the examined tissues/organs.
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 14A.

claim: Fshr is expressed in all examined tissues/organs as demonstrated by ddRT-PCR.
source: We also obtained total RNA from the following tissues: lung, kidney, thoracic vertebra, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, skeletal muscle, tails, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, thyroid, brain, pancreas, and duodenum. After reversing mRNA from total RNA, we performed ddRT-PCR with mouse-specific primers to check Fshr expression at the transcriptional level as described in the Methods section. The results demonstrated Fshr expression in these tissues, and the expression profile was categorized into three groups: (1) high expression in the lung and kidney tissues; (2) moderate expression in the thoracic (T) vertebrae, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, and muscle; and (3) low expression in the tail, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, brain, pancreas, and duodenum (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is supported by the ddRT-PCR data shown in Figure 14B.

claim: High Fshr expression was found in the lung and kidney tissues by ddRT-PCR.
source: The results demonstrated Fshr expression in these tissues, and the expression profile was categorized into three groups: (1) high expression in the lung and kidney tissues; (2) moderate expression in the thoracic (T) vertebrae, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, and muscle; and (3) low expression in the tail, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, brain, pancreas, and duodenum (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is supported by the ddRT-PCR data shown in Figure 14B.

claim: Moderate Fshr expression was found in the thoracic (T) vertebrae, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, and muscle by ddRT-PCR.
source: The results demonstrated Fshr expression in these tissues, and the expression profile was categorized into three groups: (1) high expression in the lung and kidney tissues; (2) moderate expression in the thoracic (T) vertebrae, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, and muscle; and (3) low expression in the tail, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, brain, pancreas, and duodenum (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is supported by the ddRT-PCR data shown in Figure 14B.

claim: Low Fshr expression was found in the tail, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, brain, pancreas, and duodenum by ddRT-PCR.
source: The results demonstrated Fshr expression in these tissues, and the expression profile was categorized into three groups: (1) high expression in the lung and kidney tissues; (2) moderate expression in the thoracic (T) vertebrae, calvaria, femur, jejunum, liver, teeth, tibia, and muscle; and (3) low expression in the tail, cartilage, skin, spleen, stomach, heart, bladder, tongue, BAT, WAT, brain, pancreas, and duodenum (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is supported by the ddRT-PCR data shown in Figure 14B.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq databases support the widespread expression pattern of Fshr.
source: Finally, we also searched Fshr expression at single-cell level in four single-cell databases including DISCO (a database of Deeply Integrated Single-Cell Omics data, https://www.immunesinglecell.org/), BioGPS (a free extensible and customizable gene annotation portal, a complete resource for gene expression and protein function, http://biogps.org/exrna/#goto=welcome), Single Cell Portal (SCP, an interactive home for single-cell genomics data, https://singlecell.broadinstitute.org/), and Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx portal, https://gtexportal.org). The selected results from these databases are presented in Appendix 1—figure 3, which further support our findings of the widespread express pattern of Fshr described as above.
evidence: This is supported by data from single-cell RNA-seq databases.

claim: Fshr expression was detected in Leydig cells by scRNA-seq in DISCO and BioGPS for human cells.
source: In particular, Fshr expression was detected in Leydig cells by scRNA-seq as seen in DISCO (https://immunesinglecell.org/genepage/FSHR) and BioGPS (http://biogps.org/#goto=genereport&id=2492) for human cells.
evidence: This is supported by data from single-cell RNA-seq databases.

claim: Fshr is not limited to previously reported cells, tissues, or organs, such as the reproductive system, osteoclasts, adipose, endothelium in tumors, and neurons in the brain, but rather has a wide expression in the cells, tissues, and organs in the body, particularly in the lung, kidney, and heart, as well as Leydig cells in the testis.
source: Taken together, these data further confirmed Fshr-ZsGreen expression patterns from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line, convincingly demonstrating that Fshr is not limited to previously reported cells, tissues, or organs, such as the reproductive system, osteoclasts, adipose, endothelium in tumors, and neurons in the brain, but rather has a wide expression in the cells, tissues, and organs in the body, particularly in the lung, kidney, and heart, as well as Leydig cells in the testis, which has not previously been recognized.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: ZsGreen is an exceptionally bright green fluorescent protein derived from a Zoanthus sp. reef coral that has been modified for high solubility, bright emission, and rapid chromophore maturation.
source: Because of its high turnover of Fshr mRNA and a difficulty in detection of Fshr expression by RT-PCR and northern blotting, in this reporter line, we utilized ZsG as a GFP reporter, as ZsGreen, also called ZsGreen1, is an exceptionally bright green fluorescent protein derived from a Zoanthus sp. reef coral (Matz et al., 1999) that has been modified for high solubility, bright emission, and rapid chromophore maturation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ZsGreen supported by a citation.

claim: ZsGreen is the brightest commercially available green fluorescent protein - up to 4× brighter than EGFP with the half-life of 26 hr.
source: ZsGreen is the brightest commercially available green fluorescent protein - up to 4× brighter than EGFP with the half-life of 26 hr - and is ideally suited for whole-cell labeling and promoter-reporter studies to indicate the promoter activity of a gene of interest, which has been used in numerous GFP reporter mice (Zhu et al., 2012b; Pippin et al., 2013; Pippin et al., 2014; Büller et al., 2015; Dewas et al., 2015; Nazareth et al., 2015; Xiao et al., 2015; Kaverina et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2016; Fougère et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ZsGreen supported by citations.

claim: The 19-amino acid P2A has the highest cleavage efficiency.
source: In addition, we also employed a short and conserved picornavirus-derived 'self-cleaving' 2A peptide to allow bicistronic expression of Fshr and ZsG, as the 19-amino acid P2A has the highest cleavage efficiency (Wang et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about P2A peptides supported by citations.

claim: The cleavage of P2A is triggered by ribosomal skipping of the peptide bond between the proline (P) and glycine (G) in C-terminal of P2A peptide.
source: The cleavage is triggered by ribosomal skipping of the peptide bond between the proline (P) and glycine (G) in C-terminal of P2A peptide, resulting in the peptide located upstream of the 2A peptide to have extra amino acids on its C-terminal end, while the peptide located downstream the 2A peptide will have an extra proline on its N-terminal end.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of P2A cleavage.

claim: P2A can nearly equalize the expression of genes upstream and downstream.
source: Therefore, P2A can nearly equalize the expression of genes upstream and downstream.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of P2A cleavage.

claim: Fshr is normally expressed without interruptions and ZsG expression indicates Fshr promoter activity in the defined cells.
source: As a result, Fshr is normally expressed without interruptions and ZsG expression indicates Fshr promoter activity in the defined cells, demonstrated by the comparison of Fshr expression in the testes and ovaries between Fshr-ZsGreen and B6 mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The P2A-ZsGreen construct was precisely inserted into the site between the last exon (exon 10) and the stop codon of the Fshr locus.
source: The P2A-ZsGreen construct was precisely inserted into the site between the last exon (exon 10) and the stop codon of the Fshr locus, which was confirmed by integration detection PCR, sequencing of PCR fragments, and Southern blotting with Fshr locus-specific enzyme restriction digestions.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation described in the methods and results.

claim: Successful insertion allows the endogenous promoter of Fshr to drive ZsGreen reporter expression.
source: Successful insertion allows the endogenous promoter of Fshr to drive ZsGreen reporter expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design of the reporter construct.

claim: Using the native regulatory element responsible for governing the expression of the target gene ensures that the expression pattern of the GFP reporter closely mirrors that of the gene of interest, Fshr, within its natural context.
source: This approach greatly enhanced our understanding of this critical cellular pathway in several ways. First, employing the native regulatory element responsible for governing the expression of the target gene ensures that the expression pattern of the GFP reporter closely mirrors that of the gene of interest, Fshr, within its natural context. Consequently, this approach provides a more faithful representation of gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using endogenous promoters.

claim: Endogenous promoters often exhibit specific spatial and temporal expression patterns, driving gene expression in specific cell types or developmental stages.
source: Second, endogenous promoters often exhibit specific spatial and temporal expression patterns, driving gene expression in specific cell types or developmental stages. This capability facilitates the capture of the dynamic nature of gene regulation and enables the study of gene expression under diverse physiological conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about endogenous promoters.

claim: Utilizing endogenous promoters minimizes potential perturbations to the native gene regulation machinery.
source: Third, utilizing endogenous promoters minimizes potential perturbations to the native gene regulation machinery. It avoids the need to introduce exogenous elements or artificial constructs, reducing the likelihood of altering the gene's expression behavior or interfering with its regulatory interactions.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using endogenous promoters.

claim: Using a tagged protein under endogenous regulation avoids fixation artifacts and allows detection of the target's activity in live cells.
source: Unlike biochemical assays or immunostaining, using a tagged protein under endogenous regulation avoids fixation artifacts and allows detection of the target's activity in live cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the reporter system.

claim: The findings of Fshr expression in Leydig cells are in line with previous works in fishes, rats, dogs, and humans performed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in situ hybridization.
source: Although this finding is different from present thoughts that Fshr is only present in Sertoli cells but not in other cell types of the testis, our finding is in line with previous works in fishes (including African catfish, zebrafish, teleosts, and Japanese eels) (García-López et al., 2009; Levavi-Sivan et al., 2010; García-López et al., 2010; Burow et al., 2020; Chauvigné et al., 2012; Ohta et al., 2007, rats An et al., 2022), dogs (Kasimanickam and Kasimanickam, 2015), and humans (Bonci et al., 2018) performed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Fshr expression in Leydig cells strongly indicates that Fsh-Fshr plays a role in the production of steroids in males.
source: Fshr expression in Leydig cells strongly indicates that Fsh-Fshr plays a role in the production of steroids in males.

claim: The low Fshr expression in TM3 cells may provide evidence on a reason that these cells do not respond well to FSH treatments.
source: It may provide an evidence on a reason that these cells do not respond well to FSH treatments (Mather, 1980), and indicates that this cell line may not be a typical Leydig cell population and new Leydig cell lines should be established in the future.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed low Fshr expression in TM3 cells and their known poor response to FSH.

claim: Fshr expression was observed in osteoclasts in frozen sections.
source: In previous reports, Fshr expression in osteoclasts was detected only by RT-PCR, western blot, and immunostaining in cultures of primary murine precursors (Sun et al., 2006; Zhu et al., 2012a; Zhu et al., 2012c). Using the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line, we visualized Fshr expression in multinucleated osteoclasts in frozen sections, clearly demonstrating Fshr expression in osteoclasts.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claim: Fshr expression was observed in cells of the osteoblast lineage, from osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts to osteocytes and bone lining cells.
source: Intriguingly, this powerful tool enabled us to examine Fshr expression in other cell types in bone. Surprisingly, we observed Fshr expression in cells of the osteoblast lineage, from osteoprogenitor cells and osteoblasts to osteocytes and bone lining cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter mice.

claim: Fsh may regulate not only osteoclast-mediated bone resorption but also osteoblasts for bone formation.
source: This finding indicates that Fsh may regulate not only osteoclast-mediated bone resorption but also osteoblasts for bone formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed Fshr expression in both osteoclasts and osteoblasts.

claim: The Fshr cKO induced in osteocytes significantly reduced Fshr expression and triggered an increase in the cortical thickness.
source: To functionally prove the presence of Fshr in osteoblasts/osteocytes, we also deleted Fshr in osteocytes in an inducible model. The Fshr cKO induced in osteocytes significantly reduce Fshr expression and triggered an increase in the cortical thickness (Figure 3D) and a much more profound increase in bone mass and a decrease in fat mass than blockade by Fsh antibodies (unpublished data), illuminating Fshr expression in the osteoblast lineage.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

source: This bright Fshr-ZsGreen is more obviously seen in large arteries, such as the ascending aorta and others located in the heart.

source: Recently, Fshr expression was reported to be present in β-cells of the pancreas to regulate glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, further supporting our findings of the Fshr expression pattern (Cheng et al., 2024).

claim: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line faithfully recapitulates endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution.
source: In summary, we established and validated an Fshr-ZsGreen protein reporter in vivo that faithfully recapitulates endogenous Fshr expression at single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental validation data.

claim: In addition to gonadal tissues, Fshr is also highly expressed in extragonadal systems, such as the lung, kidney, heart, and pancreas.
source: Our compelling findings reveal that in addition to gonadal tissues, Fshr is also highly expressed in extragonadal systems, such as the lung, kidney, heart, and pancreas.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: The Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line is a powerful tool for detecting the location of Fshr expression.
source: Although the Fshr-ZsGreen reporter line is a powerful tool for detecting the location of Fshr expression, it is limited in the definition of individual isoforms of Fshr transcripts and the detection of their turnover, which should be addressed by specific antibodies and determined by the rates of transcription and RNA degradation, including Xrn1 for 5'-to-3' degradation, exosomes for 3'-to-5' degradation, and nonsense-mediated decay (Wada and Becskei, 2017; Kaverina et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the reporter system.
